title: The foreigner's prayer (1 Kings 8:41–43)
hook: Solomon asks that a stranger's prayer in the Temple be heard too

segments.voice: Yesterday, Solomon said no house could hold God. Your line was a place to turn toward. Where did you notice it reaching? Today, in the same prayer, he makes room for someone who isn't part of his people at all. Day seven hundred sixty-one.

Somebody arrives from far away. Different clothes, a different accent, maybe a different language. They've heard about this place and walked a long road to reach it. Now they stand in the courtyard among people who know the customs, and they don't. They pray anyway. Who is that prayer for? Will anyone listen? Solomon's dedication prayer, in the middle of asking for his own people, stops to answer exactly that question. Today's word belongs to that traveler.
screen: `SOMEBODY FROM FAR AWAY.` → `A LONG ROAD TO GET HERE.` → `WHO HEARS THEIR PRAYER?`

segments.voice: First Kings eight, verses forty-one to forty-three. Solomon has prayed for Israel in defeat, in drought, in famine and plague. Then he turns to someone else: the foreigner, in Hebrew the nochri, who is not of Israel but comes out of a far country for the sake of God's name. They have heard, the text says, of God's great name, strong hand and outstretched arm. And Solomon asks: when this stranger comes and prays toward this house, hear in heaven, and do according to all that the stranger calls to you for. Why? So that all the peoples of the earth may know God's name. There's a detail later readers noticed. For Israel, Solomon asks God to give each person according to their ways, since God knows the heart. For the foreigner, he asks God to do according to all that they call for. The commentator Rashi reads that difference as care. Someone of Israel knows the relationship and can bear an answer of no. But a foreigner who is turned away might say, I came all this way to that house, and I wasn't heard. So, Rashi says, Solomon asked that the stranger be answered in full. Later, the prophet Isaiah will speak of God's house as a house of prayer for all peoples. And the Torah tells Israel to care for the stranger, because they were strangers in the land of Egypt. So this is no side note. The house is built by one people, and it is open to another's voice. Solomon builds walls around a courtyard, and then asks that whoever walks into it be heard.
screen: `NOCHRI: THE FOREIGNER.` · `DO ALL THAT THE STRANGER ASKS.` · `RASHI: SO NO ONE GOES HOME UNHEARD.` · `A HOUSE OF PRAYER FOR ALL PEOPLES.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: pray for a stranger. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind someone you don't know: a person you passed on the street, a new family down the block, someone far from home whose story you heard. You don't need their name. Just hold them for a moment. What might they be asking for tonight? Safety, work, a place to belong. If you pray, you can ask, in Solomon's spirit, that their prayer be heard. If you don't, just wish them well, plainly, for the length of this sit. The bell holds the time.
Nochri. The Hebrew word for a foreigner, the stranger from a far country Solomon asked God to hear fully. Today's word.
Your line: hear the stranger too. Today, when a newcomer speaks, at work, in a line, in a group chat, give them your full attention. Day seven hundred sixty-one.

howItsDone: Jews read Solomon's prayer for the foreigner in the book of Kings alongside the Torah's command to care for the stranger, and commentators such as Rashi ask why the foreigner's prayer is to be answered in full.

fork.setup: you're dedicating your people's holy house. someday a foreigner may come to pray there. what do you ask?
options: that only your own people be heard here.
that the foreigner's prayer be heard in full.
that the foreigner first become one of your people.
fork.reveal: Solomon asked God to do according to all that the stranger calls for, so that all the peoples of the earth may know God's name.

original.note: Hebrew: a foreigner, someone from another land. the nochri of Solomon's prayer.

trapdoor: what you thought: the Temple was only for Israel.
what it means: Solomon asks that a foreigner's prayer toward the house be heard in full.
what a scholar hears: Rashi notes Israel is answered by their ways, but the stranger gets all they ask, so they won't feel unheard.

notes: All scripture here is paraphrased; no direct quotation.
Rashi on 1 Kings 8:43 (drawing on midrash): Israel is answered according to their ways, the foreigner in full, lest he complain he was not heard. Please confirm the reading.
Exodus verse numbering differs between Hebrew (22:20) and some English Bibles (22:21).
Editor: corrected the order of the prayer (exile, 8:46, comes after the foreigner, 8:41; before it come defeat, drought, famine and plague) and matched Isaiah 56:7 ('my house', not 'this house').
